title: Chapter 23 — Which Is The Most Warlike And Most Revolutionary Class In Democratic Armies?
paragraphs: It is part of the essence of a democratic army to be very numerous relative to the people it belongs to, as I will show later. On the other hand, people living in democratic times rarely choose a military life. Democratic nations are therefore soon led to give up voluntary recruiting and adopt compulsory enlistment. The necessity of their social condition forces them to the latter, and it is easy to foresee that they will all eventually adopt it. When military service is compulsory, the burden is borne indiscriminately and equally by the whole community. This is another necessary consequence of the social condition of these nations, and of their ideas. The government may do almost whatever it pleases, provided it appeals to the whole community at once: it is the unequal distribution of the weight, not the weight itself, which usually occasions resistance. But since military service is common to all citizens, the obvious consequence is that each remains on active duty for only a few years. So it lies in the nature of things that in democracies the soldier only passes through the army, whereas among most aristocratic nations the military profession is one that the soldier adopts — or that is imposed on him — for life.

This has important consequences. Among the soldiers of a democratic army, some acquire a taste for military life, but the majority, enlisted against their will and always ready to go back to their homes, do not consider themselves seriously engaged in the military profession, and are always thinking of leaving it. Such men do not contract the needs, and only half share the passions, that this mode of life breeds. They adapt themselves to their military duties, but their minds remain attached to the interests and duties that occupied them in civilian life. They do not, therefore, imbibe the spirit of the army — or rather, they infuse the spirit of the community at large into the army, and keep it there. Among democratic nations the private soldiers remain most like civilians: on them the habits of the nation have the firmest hold, and public opinion the greatest influence. It is through the private soldiers especially that it may be possible to infuse into a democratic army the love of freedom and the respect of rights, once these principles have been successfully instilled in the people at large. The reverse happens among aristocratic nations, where the soldiery eventually have nothing in common with their fellow citizens, and live among them as strangers, often as enemies. In aristocratic armies the officers are the conservative element, because the officers alone have kept a strict connection with civil society, and never give up the purpose of resuming their place in it sooner or later. In democratic armies the private soldiers hold this position, and for the same reason.

It often happens, by contrast, that in these same democratic armies the officers acquire tastes and needs wholly distinct from those of the nation — a fact that can be accounted for as follows. Among democratic nations, the man who becomes an officer severs all the ties that bound him to civilian life; he leaves it forever, and has no interest in returning. His true country is the army, since he owes everything he has to the rank he has reached in it; he therefore follows the fortunes of the army, rises or sinks with it, and from then on directs all his hopes to that quarter alone. Since the needs of an officer are distinct from those of the country, he may ardently desire war, or labor to bring about a revolution, at the very moment when the nation most desires stability and peace. There are, nevertheless, some causes that allay this restless and warlike spirit. Though ambition is universal and continual among democratic nations, we have seen that it is seldom great. A man who, born in the lower classes of the community, has risen from the ranks to become an officer, has already taken a prodigious step. He has gained a footing in a sphere above the one he filled in civilian life, and he has acquired rights that most democratic nations will always consider inalienable. *a He is willing to pause after so great an effort and enjoy what he has won. The fear of risking what he has already obtained dampens the desire to acquire what he has not. Having conquered the first and greatest obstacle to his advancement, he resigns himself with less impatience to the slowness of his progress. His ambition will cool more and more as the growing distinction of his rank teaches him that he has more to put at risk. If I am not mistaken, the least warlike — and also the least revolutionary — part of a democratic army will always be its chief commanders. [Footnote a: The position of officers is indeed much more secure among democratic nations than elsewhere; the lower the personal standing of the man, the greater is the comparative importance of his military grade, and the more just and necessary that the enjoyment of that rank be secured by the laws.]

But the remarks I have just made about officers and soldiers do not apply to a numerous class that fills the intermediate space between them in every army — I mean the class of non-commissioned officers. This class of non-commissioned officers, which has never played a part in history until the present century, is, I think, from now on destined to play one of some importance. Like the officers, non-commissioned officers have broken, in their minds, all the ties that bound them to civilian life; like them, they devote themselves permanently to the service, and perhaps make it even more exclusively the object of all their desires. But non-commissioned officers are men who have not yet reached a firm and lofty post where they can pause and breathe more freely before attaining further promotion. By the very nature of his duties, which is invariable, a non-commissioned officer is doomed to lead an obscure, confined, comfortless, and precarious existence. So far he sees nothing of military life but its dangers; he knows nothing of it but its privations and its discipline — harder to bear than dangers. He suffers all the more from his present miseries because he knows that the constitution of society and of the army permits him to rise above them; he may, indeed, at any time obtain his commission, and enter at once into command, honors, independence, rights, and enjoyments. Not only does this object of his hopes appear to him of immense importance, but he is never sure of reaching it until it is actually his own. The grade he holds is by no means irrevocable; he is always entirely at the arbitrary pleasure of his commanding officer, for this is imperiously required by the necessity of discipline. A slight fault, a whim, may at any moment deprive him of the fruits of many years of toil and striving. Until he reaches the grade to which he aspires, he has accomplished nothing; only on reaching that grade does his career seem to begin. A desperate ambition cannot fail to be kindled in a man thus incessantly goaded on by his youth, his wants, his passions, the spirit of his age, his hopes, and his fears. Non-commissioned officers are therefore bent on war — on war always, and at any cost; but if war is denied them, then they desire revolutions that suspend the authority of established regulations, and enable them, aided by the general confusion and the political passions of the time, to get rid of their superior officers and take their places. Nor is it impossible for them to bring about such a crisis, because their common origin and habits give them considerable influence over the soldiers, however different their passions and desires may be.

It would be a mistake to suppose that these various characteristics of officers, non-commissioned officers, and men belong to any particular time or country; they will always occur, at all times, and among all democratic nations. In every democratic army the non-commissioned officers will be the worst representatives of the pacific and orderly spirit of the country, and the private soldiers the best. The latter will carry into military life the strength or weakness of the manners of the nation; they will display a faithful reflection of the community. If that community is ignorant and weak, they will let themselves be drawn by their leaders into disturbances, either unconsciously or against their will; if it is enlightened and energetic, the community will itself keep them within the bounds of order.
